OIIX.name: FIR Tehran
OIIX.conflictType: Interstate conflict — Iran vs Israel/US (fragile ceasefire)
OIIX.narrative: EASA's CZIB-2026-04 reflects a ceasefire that has held since April 2026 but remains fragile, with an elevated Iranian air-defence posture that raises the risk of civil aircraft being misidentified. EASA has warned escalation could resume with little notice. Eastern OIIX was partially reopened for overflights in June 2026 while western Iran remains closed; a small number of specific temporary routes above FL285 link Oman/UAE with Central Asia, the Caucasus and Turkey. Several radar systems remain degraded and many western airports are still closed or daytime-only. The shoot-down of Ukraine International Airlines flight 752 over Tehran in Jan 2020 illustrates how quickly misidentification risk can materialise. Key timeline: March 2026 — FIR closed following large-scale US and Israeli strikes and Iranian missile/drone retaliation; June 2026 — eastern portion partially reopened; July 2026 — EASA CZIB continues to advise against operations at any altitude following renewed military activity.

cross.detail: Some overflights above FL285 are possible via specific temporary routes, but western Iran remains heavily restricted, radar systems are degraded, and virtually all operators continue to avoid the airspace.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Most Europe-Asia traffic routes south via Egypt/Saudi or north via the Caucasus/Afghanistan. Several states continue to warn against operations in Iranian airspace. Earlier timeline milestones: June 2025 — Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes; Oct 2024 — mutual missile attacks led most operators to avoid both airspaces.

ORBB.name: FIR Baghdad
ORBB.conflictType: Non-state armed groups (IBMGs) + Iranian missile/drone spillover
ORBB.narrative: Despite the regional ceasefire, EASA cites recurrent Iranian drone and ballistic-missile strikes reaching Iraqi airspace, alongside the continued presence of Iranian-backed militant groups (IBMGs), as reasons the Baghdad FIR remains a do-not-operate zone. The primary risks are missile and drone activity linked to regional conflicts, misidentification by air-defence systems operated by local and foreign military forces, and terrorist groups possessing portable anti-aircraft weaponry. ORBB was closed in March 2026 following US and Israeli strikes on Iran and subsequent Iranian retaliation, then reopened to overflights in June 2026 following the ceasefire, with north-south routes available through the FIR. Earlier incidents: June 2025 — airspace closed as missiles and drones transited Iraqi airspace during Israeli-Iranian exchange; Apr 2024 — closed due to Iranian drone and missile strike on Israel; Apr 2023 — drone and missile attacks in northern Iraq near ORSU and ORER; Oct 2021 — US operators permitted above FL320 under updated FAA restrictions.

cross.detail: Iraq is open for overflights, but most operators still consider ORBB too high risk. Some airlines are using it; main traffic flows remain north via the Caucasus/Afghanistan or south via Egypt/Saudi/Oman.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Iraqi airspace remains open and some operators continue using it, but most Europe-Asia traffic still routes around it. EASA continues to advise operators not to operate in the ORBB/Baghdad FIR at any altitude under its current CZIB.

OLBB.name: FIR Beirut
OLBB.narrative: A Trilateral Framework Agreement between Israel, Lebanon and the US (26 June 2026) is a step toward consolidating the ceasefire, but EASA notes its long-term implementation is uncertain, and that Lebanon has not shown it can proactively manage airspace risk. Israeli airstrikes in Lebanon continued from Feb through Jul 2026 despite repeated ceasefire extensions. GNSS spoofing and jamming have been reported in the OLBB/Beirut FIR since Nov 2023. Some states allow limited operations to OLBA/Beirut provided arrivals and departures remain over the Mediterranean Sea.

cross.detail: July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military activity around the Strait of Hormuz. Israeli airstrikes in Lebanon continue and most international operators continue to avoid the airspace. Several states maintain long-standing warnings, and EASA continues to advise operators not to operate in the OLBB/Beirut FIR at any altitude. Oct 2024: Israel launched a ground operation against Hezbollah in southern Lebanon.

OJAC.name: FIR Amman
OJAC.conflictType: Missile/drone overflight risk (regional spillover, no direct conflict on Jordanian soil)
OJAC.narrative: Jordan's airspace has repeatedly seen Iranian missiles and drones pass through en route to other targets, intercepted by Jordanian and allied air defences. Jordanian authorities have not published any airspace restrictions of their own despite this activity. Jordan remained open throughout the Feb–Jul 2026 Iran conflict period, although missile and drone activity affected several neighbouring countries. EASA issued an Information Note in July 2026 advising operators to take the potential risk into account before operating in the OJAC/Amman FIR following renewed military activity in the Gulf. Jordan temporarily closed its airspace during the Iranian drone and missile attack on Israel in Apr 2024, and intercepted drones and missiles transiting its airspace during regional escalation in Oct 2023.

cross.detail: Open and operating normally, though not a major transit route for Europe-Asia traffic. Most operators continue to route via Egypt and Saudi Arabia.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. Jordan airspace remains open and operating normally. The primary risk is missile and drone activity linked to regional conflicts; there have been no significant downgrades to recent airspace warnings.

OKAC.name: FIR Kuwait
OKAC.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OKAC.narrative: Kuwait hosts major US military facilities, making it a plausible target for Iranian retaliation and increasing the risk of civil aircraft being caught up in an attack or an air-defence response. Missile and drone strikes damaged OKKK/Kuwait airport in March 2026. The OKAC/Kuwait FIR closed and reopened several times during the Feb–Jul 2026 Iran conflict and is currently open for arrivals and departures only, with overflights remaining prohibited. EASA issued a CZIB in July 2026 advising operators not to operate in the FIR at any altitude.

cross.detail: Kuwait has extended its airspace restrictions until at least Aug 4. Overflights through the OKAC/Kuwait FIR are still not permitted — only flights arriving to or departing from OKKK/Kuwait are allowed, with prior approval.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. Kuwait has been directly affected by strikes at OKKK/Kuwait airport and other military targets. The FIR remains open for arrivals and departures only; overflights continue to be prohibited. No significant downgrades to recent airspace warnings.

OBBB.name: FIR Bahrain
OBBB.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OBBB.narrative: As with Kuwait and Qatar, the US military presence in Bahrain is the main driver of EASA's risk assessment for this FIR. The OBBB/Bahrain FIR closed and reopened several times during the Feb–Jul 2026 Iran conflict before returning to normal overflight operations. Iranian missile and drone attacks targeted several Gulf states in March 2026, with incidents affecting airspace around Bahrain. EASA issued a CZIB in July 2026 advising operators not to operate in the FIR at any altitude.

cross.detail: Bahrain is open to overflights again. Note that nearby Kuwait remains restricted, which can affect routing. EASA advises operators to avoid the FIR at all levels.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. Bahrain airspace remains open to overflights. Bahrain lies close to several key military facilities in the Gulf; no significant downgrades to recent airspace warnings. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings across the region.

OTDF.name: FIR Doha
OTDF.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OTDF.narrative: Qatar hosts significant US forces and has itself been targeted by Iranian strikes during the recent escalation, keeping it on EASA's do-not-operate list even as operational conditions ease. A missile strike was reported at Al Udeid Air Base near Doha in March 2026. The OTDF/Doha FIR closed and reopened several times during the Feb–Jul 2026 Iran conflict before returning to largely normal overflight operations. EASA issued a CZIB in July 2026 advising operators not to operate in the FIR at any altitude.

cross.detail: Qatar has reopened to overflights; earlier restrictions on waypoints and arrival/departure route segments have been withdrawn, though some temporary restricted areas and military activity remain. Operationally near-normal, but EASA advises operators to avoid the FIR at all levels.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. Qatar airspace remains open and operating largely normally. Qatar was directly affected during the conflict, including missile strikes near Doha; no significant downgrades to recent airspace warnings.

OMAE.name: FIR Emirates
OMAE.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OMAE.narrative: The UAE's proximity to the Strait of Hormuz and its role as a regional hub keep it firmly within EASA's risk assessment, despite being operationally busy.

cross.detail: The UAE remains open to overflights, with traffic managed through normal ATS routes and temporary RNAV corridors. GPS interference continues to be a significant operational issue across the FIR. EASA advises operators to avoid the FIR at all levels.

OOMM.name: FIR Muscat — west of 58°E only
OOMM.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OOMM.narrative: Unlike other Gulf FIRs, only the western portion of Omani/Gulf of Oman waters is covered — reflecting where commercial vessel attacks and Strait of Hormuz tension actually concentrate. Oman remained open throughout the Feb–Jul 2026 Iran conflict and became a key part of the main southern bypass route (Egypt-Saudi-Oman) for Europe-Asia traffic, with ongoing GNSS interference reports. EASA's current CZIB advises operators not to operate over the waters of the Gulf of Oman within the OOMM/Muscat FIR west of 58°E.

cross.detail: Oman remains one of the most useful FIRs in the region for the southern bypass. It is open but part of the managed corridor system, with flow measures and ongoing GNSS interference reports.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Oman airspace remains open and carries significant Europe-Asia overflight traffic on the southern bypass. The primary risk is spillover of missile or drone activity from conflicts elsewhere in the region. Oct 2024: Israel and Iran carried out missile attacks against each other, leading many operators to avoid airspace between the two countries.

OSTT.name: FIR Damascus
OSTT.narrative: EASA's longest-running Middle East bulletin (19 revisions since 2017) reflects a still-unresolved multi-actor conflict. Traffic patterns have shifted: OSTT quietly reopened to some regional carriers in early 2025 as an alternative to the more restricted Iran/Iraq corridor, even though most Western operators continue to avoid it. The primary risks are military activity linked to the Syrian conflict — including Israeli airstrikes targeting Iranian and Hezbollah-linked positions — and the potential for misidentification by air-defence systems. OSTT/Damascus FIR was closed in March 2026 following US and Israeli strikes on Iran and subsequent Iranian retaliation, then saw a gradual increase in overflights from Jan–Jul 2026 as some regional operators used it as an alternative to Iran and Iraq. Syrian airspace was temporarily closed in Dec 2024 following the fall of the Assad regime. Earlier incidents: Oct 2023 — airstrikes damaged runways at OSDI/Damascus and OSAP/Aleppo; Feb 2020 — an A320 approaching Damascus diverted after being caught in crossfire during Israeli airstrikes; Sep 2018 — a Russian IL-20 was shot down in error near the Syria-Cyprus FIR boundary.

cross.detail: Syria has quietly become part of the regional routing picture again after years of almost no international overflight traffic.

July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action around the Strait of Hormuz. Syrian airspace remains high risk, though some regional operators have started using it as an alternative to restricted Iran/Iraq routing. Several countries continue to prohibit or advise against operations in the OSTT/Damascus FIR due to military operations, anti-aviation weaponry and unstable security conditions.

OYSC.name: FIR Sana'a only
OYSC.conflictType: Civil war + interstate spillover (Red Sea attacks)
OYSC.narrative: This bulletin covers only the Sana'a FIR, not the whole of Yemen. The ongoing civil war and Houthi involvement in the wider regional conflict keep the risk assessment unchanged since 2017.

cross.detail: Yemen remains an active conflict zone; the vast majority of Yemeni airspace (OYSC/Sanaa FIR) should be avoided. Several countries prohibit overflying any land portion of the FIR. US operators can use offshore routes UT702 and M999; others permit flights on overwater portions. The primary risk is intentional targeting by terrorist groups with sophisticated anti-aircraft weaponry, including explosive drones and missiles. Saudi and Israeli airstrikes can occur at any time, including in the capital Sana'a. Major events: Jul 2026 — Yemen's government carried out an airstrike on the runway at OYSN/Sanaa Airport to stop an Iranian aircraft from landing. Dec 2024 - ongoing — OYSN/Sanaa Airport closed due to damage from Israeli airstrikes in Dec 2024 and May 2025. Jan 2024 — US and UK carried out airstrikes against Houthi rebels in response to missile and drone attacks in the Red Sea. Sep 2023 — Houthi drone attacks near the Yemen-Saudi border. Apr-Oct 2022 — All parties agreed a ceasefire. 2018-2022 — Frequent Saudi airstrikes on Sanaa and other targets in retaliation for Houthi drone attacks. 2017 — OYSN/Sanaa Airport badly damaged by coalition airstrikes.

UUWV.name: FIR Moscow and others (west of 60°E)
UUWV.conflictType: Interstate war — Russian invasion of Ukraine (air-defence risk)
UUWV.narrative: Issued after the likely accidental shoot-down of Azerbaijan Airlines flight 8243 near Grozny in December 2024, this bulletin reflects the risk that Russian air-defence systems responding to Ukrainian strikes pose to civil aircraft, compounded by widespread GNSS interference.

cross.detail: As of June 2025, drone attacks across Russia are ramping up, with some reaching as far as Siberia, increasing risk for any aircraft still using Russian airspace. Hundreds of drones have been shot down recently, including in areas around Moscow. Russian air-defence systems using surface-to-air missiles capable of reaching all altitudes means the risk applies at every level. Daytime disruptions are now common alongside the more frequent night-time activity. Ukraine's airspace has remained fully closed to civil aviation since Feb 2022. The primary risk is unintended targeting of civil aircraft by military near the Russia-Ukraine border, including misidentification (as with MAS17, UIA752). Major events: Jan 2025 — EASA issued a new CZIB recommending against flights in western Russia (west of 60°E) due to misidentification risk from air-defence systems targeting Ukrainian drones and missiles, following the shoot-down of a passenger jet at URMG/Grozny on Dec 25. Jan 2024 — military transport aircraft crashed near Belgorod, approx 20nm from the Ukrainian border; both sides accused each other of shooting it down. Aug 2023 — private jet carrying Wagner chief Yevgeny Prigozhin crashed en route from Moscow to St Petersburg on Aug 23. Jul 2023 - ongoing — drone strikes on Moscow and surrounding region; Moscow airports forced to close temporarily on multiple occasions, with frequency increasing.

UKBV.name: All Ukrainian FIRs
UKBV.narrative: In force since the day of the invasion, this remains one of the clearest and most stable prohibitions in this dataset — Ukraine itself has closed its FIRs to civil traffic by NOTAM.

cross.detail: Ukraine closed its entire airspace to all civil traffic on Feb 24, 2022, due to a military invasion by Russia. There is ongoing active conflict between Russian and Ukrainian forces. Russia, Belarus and Moldova have closed large sections of their own airspace near FIR boundaries with Ukraine. All major countries that regularly issue airspace warnings (the US, UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy) have issued total flight bans for Ukraine. The primary risk is unintended targeting of civil aircraft by military, including misidentification (as with MAS17, UIA752). The secondary risk is potential loss of Ukrainian ATC service at short notice (e.g. cyber attack) and other unforeseeable non-normal operating environments. Prior to February 2022, concerns centred on the conflict in eastern Ukraine (UKDV/Dnipro FIR) and the contested ATC and airspace in Crimea (UKFV/URFV/Simferopol FIR).

HSSS.name: FIR Khartoum
HSSS.conflictType: Civil war — Sudan Armed Forces (SAF) vs Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
HSSS.narrative: The ongoing SAF–RSF civil war has put anti-aircraft artillery, MANPADS and SAM systems into play across the whole of Sudanese airspace, keeping the entire Khartoum FIR off-limits.

cross.detail: Following a military coup in April 2023, Sudan remains closed to all civilian flights. HSSK/Khartoum airport is closed, but no NOTAMs are being issued. A Contingency Plan with published overflight routes via HSPN/Port Sudan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and South Sudan is available. In South Sudan, air navigation services remain suspended above FL245. Several countries have issued warnings advising operators not to enter Sudanese airspace due to risks from anti-aircraft weaponry and military activity. The primary risk is security on the ground for any unplanned diversions; throughout the conflict, passenger jets have been targeted by gunfire at HSSK/Khartoum Airport. The secondary risk is Sudan's proximity to South Sudan, which has poor ATC provision below FL245. Major events: Nov 2025 — Il-76 reportedly shot down by a surface-to-air missile near Babanusa, southern Sudan. May 2025 — drone attack targeting critical infrastructure including HSPN/Port Sudan airport. Oct 2024 — foreign-registered cargo aircraft shot down by local militia over North Darfur, near the Chad border. Apr 2023 — military coup on Apr 15; Sudan's airspace closed, South Sudan's airspace closed above FL245. Oct 2021 — military coup on Oct 25; HSSK/Khartoum airport closed for two days.

HLLL.name: FIR Tripoli
HLLL.narrative: Libya's two rival governments and various non-state armed actors create a real risk of misidentification when crossing between areas controlled by different authorities. The one carve-out is for coastal airport approaches made from over the sea.
HLLL.restrictionLabel: Do not operate, except flights to coastal airports approached from the sea, subject to ATC contact and your own risk assessment

cross.detail: A civil war has been ongoing since 2014. Some progress was made in Oct 2020 with a new government, but Libya remains an active conflict zone with armed clashes between rival militia groups. The primary risk is misidentification by Libyan air-defence systems, or by militia who have threatened to shoot down aircraft in western Libya including at HLLM/Tripoli Mitiga airport. Military activity has been reported over the high seas operating outside ATC. Reliable ATC services cannot be guaranteed, with regular radar and ATS outages and severe VHF limitations across the HLLL FIR. Risk remains high at all flight levels. Major events: Aug 2023 — major evacuation of aircraft from Tripoli due to violent clashes and gunfire at Mitiga airport. Jul 2023 — Italy cancelled its 10-year ban on flights to/from Libya. Aug 2022 — militia air-defence forces claimed to have shot down a US drone near Benghazi. Jun 2022 — failed militia attempt to seize Tripoli government offices; armed clashes and suspension of flights at HLLM/Mitiga. Jan 2020 — multiple airstrikes targeting HLLM/Mitiga airport. Nov 2019 — militia advancing on Tripoli declared a no-fly-zone, threatening to shoot down civil aircraft at HLLM/Mitiga. 2014 — HLLT/Tripoli airport closed after militia clashes destroyed most facilities; remains closed.

DRRR.name: Malian territory, especially the north-east
DRRR.conflictType: Insurgency — non-state armed groups active across the Sahel
DRRR.narrative: Non-state armed groups operating in Mali, particularly in the north-east, are assessed to have MANPADS and SAM missile capability, which is why the restriction is altitude-based rather than a total ban.

cross.detail: The conflict in northern and central Mali has continued since 2012 and the security situation remains volatile. Several countries have warnings in place, typically advising operations at or above FL250 or FL260 and avoiding GATB/Timbuktu, GAGO/Gao and GAKL/Kidal. The US advises caution at all levels due to ongoing fighting, expanding militant activity, and a state-run paramilitary force operating anti-aircraft systems, military aircraft, UAS and electronic warfare equipment. The primary risks include MANPADS and other surface-to-air weapons, indirect fire near airports, and the potential for misidentification or military spillover. ATS for overflights of Mali is provided by the GOOO/Dakar and DRRR/Niamey FIRs, with a long-standing restriction to published ATS routes at FL320 and above. Major events: April 2026 — security situation escalated sharply; on April 25, coordinated armed attacks targeted state and military sites nationwide, with gunfire and explosions near GABS/Bamako; France issued a warning advising French operators not to operate to/from GABS or use it as an alternate. Sep 2024 — insurgents breached GABS/Bamako, set the presidential jet on fire, and the airport closed temporarily. Dec 2023 — Germany prohibited operations below FL260 in northern Mali; commercial flights to GATB/Timbuktu cancelled after shelling near the airport; a military jet crashed near GAGO/Gao, possibly shot down. Aug 2020 — all airports closed for two days during a military coup; Bamako ACC remained operational and overflights were unaffected. Apr 2018 — militants attacked UN bases near GATB/Timbuktu with indirect fire and vehicle bombs. Jan 2017 and Nov 2016 — vehicle bomb and rocket attacks targeted GAGO/Gao and GATB/Timbuktu airports.

HCSM.name: Somali airspace
HCSM.conflictType: Insurgency — Al-Shabaab and related terrorist groups
HCSM.narrative: Terrorist organisations operating in Somalia are assessed to have confirmed anti-aircraft weaponry, possibly including MANPADS, driving the same FL260 altitude floor as Mali.

cross.detail: The situation on the ground is highly unstable with ongoing attacks from extremist militants showing intent to target aviation. The primary risk is to overflying aircraft at lower flight levels, which may be targeted by anti-aircraft-capable weapons. The US prohibits flights across the HCSM/Mogadishu FIR below FL260, except for transits over the overwater portion going to/from HDAM/Djibouti. Several other countries advise against operating below FL260. A secondary risk involves aircraft being contacted by unauthorised ATC units issuing instructions that conflict with official Mogadishu Control clearances. From Nov 2025, Somaliland has required a PPR from its own CAA for all overflights, while Somalia has reaffirmed through an AIC that it controls the entire FIR — expect conflicting permit instructions near Hargeisa and northern Somalia. Major events: Feb 2024 — multiple crew reports of a 'fake controller' on the Mogadishu frequency issuing conflicting instructions. Aug 2023 — reports of uncontrolled combat helicopters flying at low levels (FL030) without position reporting. Oct 2022 — Somalian government warned HCMM/Mogadishu airport may be targeted by militant groups. May 2022 — Class A airspace implemented in the HCSM/Mogadishu FIR above FL245. 2020-ongoing — multiple Al-Shabaab attacks on HCMM/Mogadishu and nearby targets, including a UN compound. May 2020 — an Embraer EMB-120 was shot down on approach to Bardale airstrip, killing all six on board, in an accidental shoot-down by Ethiopian forces combating Al-Shabaab.

OPKR.name: Baluchistan province (partial)
OPKR.conflictType: Insurgency (violent non-state actors) + Kashmir territorial dispute
OPKR.narrative: Violent non-state actor (VNSA) groups with confirmed MANPADS operate in Baluchistan. The Kashmir dispute separately raises misidentification risk further north.

cross.detail: Tensions between Pakistan and India in the disputed Kashmir region, along with longstanding militant activity in parts of western Pakistan, create an ongoing risk in the OPKR/Karachi and OPLR/Lahore FIRs. In May 2025 there was a period of intense cross-border shelling and aerial activity in Kashmir; a ceasefire has largely held since then but the situation remains fragile. Several states and EASA maintain altitude-based restrictions, generally advising operators to remain at or above FL260. The primary risks are from anti-aviation weaponry (including potential MANPADS) below FL260, and inadvertent risk from military activity or misidentification in the Kashmir region. Major events: Feb 2026 — cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; no new airspace closures issued and commercial traffic continues to transit OAKX/Kabul FIR via P500 and G500. May 2025 — four days of cross-border strikes and shelling between India and Pakistan in Kashmir; ceasefire announced 10 May has largely held; some operators temporarily rerouted south via the Gulf of Oman and UAE. Jan 2024 — Iran conducted missile and drone strikes against a militant group in western Pakistan. Dec 2023 - ongoing — crew reports of GPS spoofing in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area, particularly around OPLA/Lahore. Feb-Aug 2019 — Pakistan closed its airspace to overflights following major clashes with India in the Kashmir region.

OPLR.name: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province (partial)
OPLR.conflictType: Insurgency (violent non-state actors) + Kashmir territorial dispute
OPLR.narrative: Covers the north-western province, where the Kashmir dispute adds a misidentification risk on top of the VNSA activity common to both restricted Pakistani provinces.

cross.detail: Tensions between Pakistan and India in the disputed Kashmir region, along with longstanding militant activity in parts of western Pakistan, create an ongoing risk in the OPKR/Karachi and OPLR/Lahore FIRs. In May 2025 there was a period of intense cross-border shelling and aerial activity in Kashmir; a ceasefire has largely held since then but the situation remains fragile. Several states and EASA maintain altitude-based restrictions, generally advising operators to remain at or above FL260. The primary risks are from anti-aviation weaponry (including potential MANPADS) below FL260, and inadvertent risk from military activity or misidentification in the Kashmir region. Major events: Feb 2026 — cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; no new airspace closures issued and commercial traffic continues to transit OAKX/Kabul FIR via P500 and G500. May 2025 — four days of cross-border strikes and shelling between India and Pakistan in Kashmir; ceasefire announced 10 May has largely held; some operators temporarily rerouted south via the Gulf of Oman and UAE. Jan 2024 — Iran conducted missile and drone strikes against a militant group in western Pakistan. Dec 2023 - ongoing — crew reports of GPS spoofing in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area, particularly around OPLA/Lahore. Feb-Aug 2019 — Pakistan closed its airspace to overflights following major clashes with India in the Kashmir region.

OAKX.name: FIR Kabul
OAKX.conflictType: Post-conflict security vacuum — extremist groups active, limited air traffic services
OAKX.narrative: Since the 2021 Taliban takeover, Afghanistan has had little to no functioning air traffic control. The Kabul FIR is Class G airspace: crews use published contingency routes and TIBA procedures rather than normal ATC clearances. Traffic through OAKX increased from March 2026 as flights used the northern bypass around the closed central Middle East corridor. Some countries limit overflights to airways P500 and G500 in the far east of the FIR; others allow the entire airspace at and above FL320. The primary risk is surface-to-air fire at low altitudes, compounded by the absence of ATC service and extreme threat to crew safety and security on the ground.

cross.detail: The OAKX/Kabul FIR remains Class G with no normal ATS service; crews must use the published contingency routes and TIBA procedures. Armenia and Azerbaijan remain important parts of the northern bypass, with steady overflight demand.

March 2026: Afghanistan's airspace remains open but has no ATC service following the US and allied forces withdrawal in Aug 2021. Traffic has increased as flights avoid the closed central Middle East corridor. Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; commercial traffic continues to transit the FIR including via P500 and G500. Aug 2021: OAKX/Kabul FIR became uncontrolled Class G airspace with no ATC service.

HAAA.name: FIR Addis Ababa, north of 8.5°N
HAAA.conflictType: Regional/border tension — assessed by EASA as medium risk
HAAA.narrative: This is an EASA Information Note, not a CZIB — meaning EASA's risk assessment group judged the risk here as medium rather than high. Full analytical detail is restricted to the CZ Hub.
HAAA.restrictionLabel: Caution only — factor into your own risk assessment and routing, below FL 260

cross.detail: The airspace risk picture in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region (the Ethiopia/Eritrea border) has improved since a peace deal in early Nov 2022, but airspace warnings remain in place. The primary risk to aviation is from large-scale ceasefire violations involving missiles or anti-aircraft weaponry — civil aircraft could be mistaken for military targets or caught in crossfire. Major events: Feb 2024 — new flare-up of fighting in the Amhara region (south of Tigray), including airstrikes. Nov 2022 — peace deal agreed in Tigray; Ethiopian Airlines planning to resume flights to HAMK/Mekele. Nov 2021 — several western countries issued airspace and travel warnings for Tigray following increased fighting. Jul 2021 — HAAA/Addis FIR closed a section of airspace below FL290 over Tigray after reports that militia shot down a military transport near Mekele. Nov 2020 — major escalation in Tigray; some airways closed by Ethiopian and Sudanese CAAs, with others very close to the conflict zone (UN321, UG300, UL432); multiple airports targeted by rockets; missiles fired into Eritrea targeting HHAS/Asmara; HABD/Bahir Dar and HAGN/Gondar also targeted. Sep 2018 — hidden ATC strike by Ethiopian controllers; inexperienced replacements brought in; strike ended Sep 7.

VYYF.name: FIR Yangon, below FL260
VYYF.conflictType: Internal armed conflict — assessed by EASA as medium risk
VYYF.narrative: As with Ethiopia, this is a medium-risk Information Note rather than a do-not-operate CZIB. France's own national guidance goes slightly further operationally, setting a hard altitude floor.
VYYF.restrictionLabel: Caution only — factor into your own risk assessment and routing, below FL 260

cross.detail: The security situation in Myanmar has deteriorated since the military coup in Feb 2021, with conflict and violence across many parts of the country, including airstrikes and armed clashes. Several countries have issued airspace warnings at lower flight levels due to risk from military operations, surface-to-air fire and anti-aviation weaponry. GPS jamming (and possible spoofing) has been reported in the north of the FIR on overflights between China and Bangladesh airspace. Major events: Jan 2024 — armed group shot down a military helicopter in the northern state of Kachin, likely using a MANPAD. Sep 2023 — rebel attacks on military targets across the country, including a makeshift drone that dropped bombs on aircraft hangars at an airbase next to VYNT/Naypyitaw airport; intermittent GPS jamming reported on airway N895. Apr 2023 — VYYY/Yangon airport temporarily closed following an improvised artillery attack by resistance groups. Sep 2022 — a Myanmar National Airlines passenger was reportedly shot as bullets passed through the fuselage of an ATR 72 on approach to VYLK/Loikaw. Feb 2021 — military coup ousted the government; ATC strike at end of Feb resulted in no ATC service for overflights; increasing strikes, protests and armed clashes with militia since then.
